title: Who Took a Bite of the Moon?
summary_zh: 月亮变细不是被咬掉了，灯和球可以帮助理解月相。
story:
Maya draws the Moon on Monday. It looks like a thin smile. Several evenings later, she draws it again. This time, the bright part looks larger.

Who is changing it? Leo asks. Perhaps someone keeps taking bites and then putting them back.

Pip searches his imaginary menu. Moon pie: one enormous serving.

Ms. Park brings a ball and a lamp into a darkened classroom. The lamp represents the Sun, and the ball represents the Moon. Maya stands in one place to be the observer on Earth.

The lamp lights half the ball. As Ms. Park moves the ball around Maya, Maya sees different amounts of the bright half.

The whole ball is still there, Maya says. I just cannot see all of its lit side from here.

Exactly, says Ms. Park. The Moon reflects sunlight. Its changing position gives us different views of its sunlit half.

Leo asks whether Earth's shadow makes the ordinary phases. Ms. Park explains that Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse when the objects line up appropriately. That is a different event.

Pip writes a notice: The Moon has not been eaten. Please cancel the emergency bakery meeting.

That evening, Maya looks up again. She draws both the bright shape she can see and a faint circle to remind herself of the whole Moon.

It is still round, she says. My view is what changes.
fact: The Moon does not make its own visible light like the Sun. We see sunlight reflected from its surface. As it orbits Earth, we see different portions of its illuminated half. These views are called phases. Ordinary Moon phases are not caused by Earth's shadow.
recap: The ball stayed whole while Maya saw different amounts of its lit half. This helped explain the Moon's changing appearance. Earth's shadow belongs in the explanation of a lunar eclipse, not the ordinary monthly phases.
phrases: It looks different tonight.
The whole object is still there.
What changes from our point of view?
question: Does the Moon actually lose a piece when it looks like a thin smile?
answer: No. We are seeing only a small part of its sunlit half from our position on Earth.
wonder: How could you keep a simple Moon diary for a week?

title: A Postcard from the Red Planet
title_zh: 来自红色星球的明信片
summary_zh: 假想一张火星明信片，区分探测器拍到的事实和想象。
story:
Leo writes a pretend postcard from Mars. Dear Maya, the beach is lovely. The trees are purple. The hotel serves excellent pancakes.

Maya reads it and laughs. How much of this is based on real information?

The postcard is real paper, Leo says.

The club decides to make a better space postcard. They look at pictures taken by robotic spacecraft. There are rocks, dust, hills, and wide landscapes. There is no pancake hotel in the photographs.

Why does Mars look reddish? Maya asks.

Ms. Park explains that iron minerals in the surface material have reacted with oxygen. Rust-colored material helps give the planet its familiar appearance.

Pip examines his wheels nervously. I prefer to keep my metal well maintained.

They learn that a rover is a robot designed to travel across a surface. It can carry cameras and scientific instruments. A rover's job is to gather information, not to invent exciting details.

Leo rewrites his card. Dear Maya, Mars has dusty, rocky landscapes. Robots help us study it. I would like to explore it someday, but I would need much more than a backpack.

What about the pancakes? Pip asks.

I will label those as imagination, says Leo.

The finished card has two sections: What we know, and What I imagine.

Maya likes it. Now the reader can enjoy the adventure without confusing the two.
fact: Mars is called the Red Planet because iron-bearing material on its surface has become oxidized, giving much of the dust a rusty color. Robotic orbiters, landers, and rovers gather different kinds of information. Pictures are evidence, but they cannot by themselves answer every question about a planet.
recap: Leo's first Mars postcard mixed invented hotels with a real planet. The club used spacecraft pictures and basic science to improve it. They kept the imaginative parts but labeled them clearly.
phrases: What is it like there?
A robot took this picture.
I would like to find out more.
question: What helps give Mars its reddish appearance?
answer: Rust-colored, oxidized iron material in its surface dust helps give it that appearance.
wonder: What would your imaginary postcard from another planet say, and which parts would be invented?

title: The Sandwich That Would Not Stay
title_zh: 不肯待在盘子里的三明治
summary_zh: 宇航员为什么漂浮？从太空午餐讲起。
story:
In a space video, an astronaut releases a small object. It floats beside her instead of dropping onto a table.

My lunch would escape, Leo says. I would spend every meal chasing it.

Pip imagines a sandwich wearing a tiny seat belt.

Maya asks a bigger question. Is there no gravity up there?

Ms. Park explains that Earth's gravity still acts strongly at the height of an orbiting space station. The station and the objects inside it are falling around Earth together.

Falling around Earth? Leo repeats.

The station also has a great deal of sideways motion. Its path curves around the planet. The astronauts and their surroundings share that motion, so the astronauts appear to float inside.

The children use an animation to follow the curved path. They do not try to reproduce it by jumping off anything.

Maya notices straps and holders in the video. Everyday objects need ways to stay in place.

An astronaut catches a floating package. Leo cheers as if she has scored a goal.

The club designs an imaginary space lunch tray. Maya adds clips for containers. Leo adds a place to hold a drink package. Pip adds a button labeled Find Missing Sandwich.

What does that button do? asks Maya.

It says, Leo, check behind you.

Leo turns around automatically. Pip is very pleased with his first successful space-lunch test.
fact: Astronauts in an orbiting station experience apparent weightlessness because they and the station are in continuous free fall around Earth. Gravity has not disappeared. This environment changes many ordinary tasks, including handling objects and eating. Securing equipment keeps useful things from drifting away.
recap: The floating object did not show that gravity was absent. The station and everything inside were falling around Earth together. The club then imagined practical ways to keep a space lunch in place.
phrases: Why does it float?
Gravity is still acting.
Let us keep it in place.
question: Has Earth's gravity disappeared where astronauts orbit?
answer: No. Their apparent weightlessness comes from falling around Earth together with their spacecraft.
wonder: Which ordinary activity would be funniest or most difficult if loose objects drifted around you?

title: A Letter Written in Starlight
summary_zh: 看星星也像收到一封很久以前寄出的信。
story:
At an evening sky event, a guide points a telescope toward a star. Maya looks through it, then steps aside for Leo.

Are we seeing the star right now? she asks.

We are receiving its light now, the guide says. But the light left the star earlier. Light travels very fast, yet space is enormous.

Leo thinks of a postcard that arrives weeks after a vacation. The picture shows an earlier moment.

That is a helpful comparison, says the guide. The delay comes from travel time.

Pip asks whether stars need stamps. The guide tells him that light delivers the information without a postal service.

They discuss an imaginary star ten light-years away. Its light would take about ten years to reach Earth. A light-year is a distance, not a unit for someone's age.

Maya looks at Leo. So you cannot say you are twelve light-years old.

I can if I am a very confused birthday cake, he replies.

The guide explains that sunlight also takes time to reach us: about eight minutes. The club enjoys the evening sky without looking directly at the Sun.

On the way home, Maya imagines the sky as a collection of messages with different delivery times.

Pip writes his own message: Dear future listener, I hope you are still curious.

Leo adds: And I hope there are snacks when the message arrives.
fact: Light takes time to travel. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. When we observe distant objects, the light shows them as they were when it began its journey. Sunlight takes roughly eight minutes to reach Earth, while light from other stars takes much longer.
recap: The telescope collected light that had traveled through space. The club compared it to a delayed letter. They learned that a light-year measures distance and that looking farther into space also means seeing older light.
phrases: How long does the journey take?
The light left earlier.
We are seeing a message from the past.
question: Is a light-year a measurement of time or distance?
answer: It is a measurement of distance: how far light travels in a year.
wonder: If you could send your future self a short message, what would you say?

title: The Puddle's Long Vacation
summary_zh: 操场上的水洼变小了，水去了哪里？
story:
After rain, a puddle sits beside the playground. Leo draws a chalk line around its edge. Later, the puddle is smaller.

Someone is stealing our puddle, he announces.

Pip begins interviewing the nearby plants. They remain suspiciously quiet.

Maya suggests another explanation. Some water may be soaking into the ground, and some may be evaporating into the air.

Ms. Park helps them think about the water cycle. Liquid water can become water vapor. The vapor is a gas that we cannot see with our eyes.

Then are clouds invisible? Leo asks.

Clouds are visible because they contain tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals, Ms. Park explains. Those are different from invisible water vapor.

They draw a pretend journey for one drop: puddle, air, cloud, rain, stream. Ms. Park reminds them that real water does not always follow that exact route. Some stays underground, in ice, or in other places for a long time.

Pip gives the imaginary drop a suitcase.

Where is it going next? he asks.

We do not know, says Maya. Our drawing shows one possible journey.

By afternoon, the chalk line surrounds mostly dry pavement.

Leo puts up a tiny sign: Puddle away on business.

Maya adds: Water still on Earth. Destination uncertain.

Pip decides that being a drop sounds exciting, but carrying a suitcase while evaporating would be difficult.
fact: Water moves among air, land, oceans, rivers, and other stores. Evaporation changes liquid water into vapor. Condensation changes vapor into tiny liquid droplets. Water can return as rain or snow. The water cycle has many routes, rather than one fixed circular trip for every drop.
recap: A shrinking puddle led to questions about evaporation and the water cycle. The club distinguished invisible water vapor from visible cloud droplets. Their traveling drop was an imaginary example of one possible route.
phrases: Where did the water go?
We cannot see the vapor.
There is more than one possible route.
question: Are the visible parts of clouds simply invisible water vapor?
answer: No. Visible clouds contain tiny water droplets or ice crystals. Water vapor itself is invisible.
wonder: Where can water stay for a long time before moving to another part of the water cycle?

title: The Rainbow That Moved Away
summary_zh: 彩虹不是固定在某处的彩色桥，为什么走近也摸不到？
story:
A rain shower ends, and sunlight appears behind the children. Ahead of them, a rainbow stretches across the sky.

Its end is near that tree, Leo says. We could walk over and see it.

They move along the path with Ms. Park. The rainbow still seems farther away.

It is escaping, says Pip. A very colorful suspect.

Ms. Park explains that a rainbow is not a solid object resting on the ground. It is an effect of light reaching their eyes from water droplets.

Sunlight contains different colors. As light enters and leaves droplets, it changes direction. Reflection inside the drops also helps send some light back toward an observer.

Maya turns around. She cannot see the same rainbow in the opposite direction.

So where I stand and where I look matter, she says.

Exactly. Your position, the sunlight, and the droplets all matter.

Leo looks at the tree again. There is no colorful door underneath it.

Pip offers to draw one. He can make a rainbow bridge that stays on paper.

The club sits under a shelter and sketches what they saw. Maya includes the Sun behind the observer and raindrops ahead.

Leo draws a little person asking a rainbow for directions.

What does the rainbow answer? Maya asks.

You can enjoy the view, Leo says, but you cannot use me as a shortcut to school.
fact: A rainbow forms when sunlight interacts with water droplets. Refraction bends the light, and reflection inside the droplets helps return it toward the observer. Different colors are separated. The rainbow you see depends on your viewpoint, so it is not a fixed object with an end you can reach.
recap: Walking toward a rainbow did not bring the children to a colored object. The rainbow was produced by light, water droplets, and their viewing position. Drawing the arrangement helped them understand the beautiful effect.
phrases: It seems to be over there.
Our position matters.
Let us look from another point of view.
question: Why could the children not walk to a solid rainbow beside the tree?
answer: A rainbow is an optical effect that depends on light, droplets, and the observer's position, not a solid object on the ground.
wonder: Where else have you seen light separate into different colors?

title: The Shadow That Changed Its Mind
summary_zh: 同一根杆子的影子，为什么一天中会改变？
story:
At nine in the morning, Maya marks the end of a pole's shadow with chalk. Leo writes the time beside the mark.

At lunchtime, they return. The shadow has moved and changed length.

The pole is walking when nobody watches, Pip suggests.

Maya checks its base. The pole has stayed in the same place.

They return once more in the afternoon and add another mark. Now their three observations tell a small story about the day.

Ms. Park explains that a shadow forms when something blocks light. The Sun's apparent position in the sky changes as Earth rotates. That changes the direction and length of the shadow.

In the classroom, they use a flashlight and a toy figure. When the light is low, the figure makes a long shadow. When the light is higher, the shadow becomes shorter.

Leo places a tiny hat on the figure. The shadow gets a hat, too.

Pip is delighted. A complete fashion show with only one model.

Maya notices that the experiment is useful but not a perfect copy of the Sun and Earth. Their flashlight is much closer than the Sun.

They place the day's marks on a drawing and label the times.

Could we use shadows to tell time? Leo asks.

People have done that with sundials, says Ms. Park.

Pip adds one condition: The clock may take a break on a cloudy day.
fact: A shadow appears where an object blocks light. Its size and direction depend on the arrangement of the light, object, and surface. Earth's rotation makes the Sun appear to move across the sky. Sundials use changing shadows to indicate time when there is suitable sunlight.
recap: The pole stayed still, but its shadow changed during the day. A flashlight model showed how light direction affects a shadow. The club used time labels to turn separate observations into a useful record.
phrases: It is shorter than before.
We measured it in the morning.
What stayed the same?
question: Did the pole need to move for its shadow to change?
answer: No. The direction of the sunlight changed as Earth rotated, so the shadow changed while the pole stayed still.
wonder: What would you need to keep the same if you wanted to compare one shadow at different times?

title: The Compass and the Stubborn Needle
summary_zh: Pip想让指南针指向零食柜，磁针却遵循自己的规则。
story:
The club prepares for a map game. Maya has a compass, and Leo has a map. Pip has already marked the snack cupboard as the most important landmark.

Why does the needle keep pointing that way? he asks.

It responds to Earth's magnetic field, Maya reads from their guide. One end points roughly toward magnetic north.

Pip rotates the compass case toward the snacks. The needle turns relative to the case and settles again.

It is very stubborn, he says.

Ms. Park brings two classroom bar magnets. The children discover that some ends pull together while others push apart.

Opposite magnetic poles attract, she explains. Like poles repel.

Leo moves a magnet near the compass. The needle changes direction.

Now it is listening to me!

It is responding to the nearby magnet, Maya says. That is why we should keep magnetic objects away when using a compass for directions.

They also learn that magnetic north and geographic north are not exactly the same. For today's simple classroom game, they use their teacher's marked directions.

Pip puts the magnet aside and follows the map properly. He reaches the reading corner.

No snacks here, he reports.

But there is a book about explorers, says Leo.

Pip chooses it. A compass can help you find a direction, he concludes, but you still have to decide where you want to go.
fact: A compass contains a small magnet that aligns with the surrounding magnetic field. Nearby magnets and some metal objects can interfere with its direction. Magnetic north is not identical to the geographic North Pole. Opposite magnetic poles attract, while like poles repel.
recap: Turning the compass case did not make the needle choose the snack cupboard. A nearby magnet did change its direction. The children learned both how a compass helps and why nearby objects can interfere.
phrases: Which way should we go?
Keep the magnet away from it.
The needle points in this direction.
question: Why did the compass needle change direction when Leo brought a magnet close?
answer: The nearby magnet changed the magnetic field affecting the needle.
wonder: If you made a map of your room, which three landmarks would help someone follow it?
